claims.text: Alcohol consumption is associated with specific causes of death including cirrhosis, alcoholism, cancers of the mouth, esophagus, pharynx, larynx, liver, breast cancer in women, and external causes in men.
Breast cancer mortality was 30 percent higher among women reporting at least one drink daily compared with nondrinkers.
Cardiovascular disease death rates were 30 to 40 percent lower among men reporting at least one drink daily compared with nondrinkers.
Cardiovascular disease death rates were 30 to 40 percent lower among women reporting at least one drink daily compared with nondrinkers.
Overall death rates were lowest among men and women reporting about one drink daily.
All-cause mortality increased with heavier drinking, particularly among adults under age 60 with lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
Alcohol consumption was associated with a small reduction in the overall risk of death in middle age (ages 35 to 69).
Smoking approximately doubled the overall risk of death in middle age.

evidence.description: Causes of death associated with drinking were cirrhosis and alcoholism; cancers of the mouth, esophagus, pharynx, larynx, and liver combined; breast cancer in women; and injuries and other external causes in men.
The mortality from breast cancer was 30 percent higher among women reporting at least one drink daily than among nondrinkers (relative risk, 1.3; 95 percent confidence interval, 1.1 to 1.6).

The rates of death from all cardiovascular diseases were 30 to 40 percent lower among men (relative risk, 0.7; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.7 to 0.8) reporting at least one drink daily than among nondrinkers.

The rates of death from all cardiovascular diseases were 30 to 40 percent lower among women (relative risk, 0.6; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.6 to 0.7) reporting at least one drink daily than among nondrinkers.
The overall death rates were lowest among men and women reporting about one drink daily.
Mortality from all causes increased with heavier drinking, particularly among adults under age 60 with lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
Alcohol consumption was associated with a small reduction in the overall risk of death in middle age (ages 35 to 69).
smoking approximately doubled this risk [of death in middle age].

methodologies.name: Prospective Cohort Study of Alcohol Consumption and Mortality
methodologies.description: A 9-year prospective follow-up study comparing cause-specific and all-cause mortality across baseline alcohol consumption levels after adjusting for risk factors.
datasets: U.S. Adults Cohort (490,000 men and women)
conditions: adjusted for risk factors including smoking habits
